subject: The Papyrus · Twenty years, one museum, and a familiar trick with the price
html:
The largest home a single civilization has ever had

On 1 November 2025, after roughly two decades of building, Egypt opened the Grand Egyptian Museum beside the Giza pyramids — the largest museum on earth devoted to a single civilization. It holds a collection of over 100,000 artifacts, with about 57,000 on display, including — for the first time ever in one place — the complete Tutankhamun collection. In its opening weeks it drew roughly 15,000–19,000 visitors a day. (Sources: Egypt State Information Service; Egypt Today.)

The price that “doubled” — sound familiar?

The museum's cost is reported at around $1–1.1 billion, up from an initial estimate near $500 million. A doubling? Partly — but a good chunk of that rise is the same trick we saw with the stock market: the Egyptian pound lost value over the long build, so the same project costs more pounds (and more dollars, as budgets were revised) without the work itself doubling. Nominal versus real, one more time — the lesson keeps coming back because it's everywhere once you look. (Source: reported figures; the cost rise is partly EGP depreciation.)

A twenty-year project, a headline price to read with care, and Tutankhamun finally under one roof. Some numbers are about money; this one's also about patience.
